questions_asked: Why do some Wordle days get far more Twitter score reports than other days? What real-world events cause the biggest surges?
Wordle's NYT version launched January 7, 2022. Roughly how big was daily Twitter score-report traffic in late 2022, and did it still grow?
Does Wordle's Hard Mode become more popular as players get more experienced with the game? Why?
What makes a Wordle word genuinely hard for players — which letter patterns, like repeated letters, trip people up most?
How often does an average Wordle player manage to solve the puzzle, versus give up after six failed guesses?
In a typical week of Wordle results, which weekday do the most players solve in just three guesses?
Which Wordle words are widely regarded as among the hardest of all, and what do they have in common?
On days when the word is especially difficult, do more players report playing in Hard Mode?
Do hard or controversial Wordle words cause more players to share their results on Twitter that day?
After a player fails a Wordle, how common is it to retry the same day or play the next day?
expert_answers:
The dominant driver is not the puzzle itself but the day of week and the news cycle. Twitter Wordle posting is a social/leisure behavior, so volume peaks on weekends and holidays and dips on ordinary weekdays; the biggest single-day surges come from external events that put Wordle in the news or give people free time — viral media coverage (e.g., the NYT acquisition announcement in early 2022, or a widely-shared controversy), holidays and long weekends, and periods of collective downtime (snowstorms, major-event cancellations, pandemic-era remote work).

Word attributes matter only secondarily: unusually hard or unusually easy words, or words with a topical/emotional hook, can lift posting because people share results when they're proud or frustrated. But these effects are smaller than calendar and news-cycle effects. So the largest surges are event-driven and calendar-driven, not word-driven.

Daily Twitter score-report volume in late 2022 was on the order of tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands of reports per day — typically around 100k–300k on ordinary days, with weekend/holiday peaks somewhat higher. This is an empirical judgment, not a precise figure.

It was no longer growing. Traffic had already peaked in early-to-mid 2022 (the viral phase around the NYT acquisition and the game's mainstream explosion), then declined and roughly plateaued through the second half of 2022. By late 2022 the trend was flat-to-slightly-declining, driven by novelty wearing off and the Twitter platform itself becoming less stable, not by continued growth.

No — Hard Mode does not become more popular as players gain experience; if anything its share is roughly flat or slowly declining over 2022.

Reasons: Hard Mode is a self-selected constraint chosen by a minority of committed players, and that population is fairly stable. It is not a skill that accumulates with practice — a casual player who has played for months has no strong incentive to switch, because Hard Mode mainly adds frustration and risk of failure, not reward. The people who adopt it tend to be the same type of player from the start (enthusiasts, purists, those seeking a challenge), so the hard-mode fraction reflects player composition more than experience.

The observed variation in the hard-mode percentage across days is driven mainly by word difficulty and by which day's player mix reports, not by a learning trend.

The biggest difficulty driver is repeated letters, especially when a letter appears twice but the player has only confirmed one instance — the feedback mechanics make it hard to realize a second copy exists. Words with two different repeated letters (e.g., EERIE, LEVEL) are hardest of all.

Next: uncommon letter positions and rare letters. Words ending in -ER, -LY, or containing Y, W, V, K, J, Q, X, Z in awkward spots narrow the candidate set slowly, because early guesses rarely confirm them.

Also hard: words that share many letters with common words but differ in one position (near-miss traps), and words with few common vowels or unusual vowel placement (e.g., vowel-heavy or vowel-light patterns).

Easier: words made of frequent letters in common positions, with no repeats, and words that are themselves common vocabulary.

These are empirical regularities from how the feedback works, not precise measurements.

The average player solves it the large majority of the time — roughly 95–98% of games end in a solve within six tries, with only about 2–5% failing (the X category). This is an empirical judgment from the reported distributions, not a precise figure.

Failure rates are higher on genuinely hard words (repeated letters, unusual patterns like EERIE), where X can rise to the high single digits or low teens, and lower on easy, common words, where X is often around 1–2%. The modal outcome is typically 3 or 4 tries, not 6, so most solves happen well before the limit.

There is no strong weekday effect on the *distribution* of solve attempts. The share solving in three tries is driven mainly by the word's difficulty, not by the day of the week.

To the extent any weekday pattern exists, it is weak and indirect: weekends and holidays bring in more casual players, who tend to need more tries, so the three-try share is if anything slightly *lower* on weekends. Ordinary weekdays, with a more committed player mix, would show a marginally higher three-try share — but the difference is small and easily swamped by word difficulty.

So: no single weekday reliably has the most three-guess solves; the modal outcome is 3–4 tries regardless of day, and word attributes dominate. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

The words most often cited as brutal are ones with repeated letters and/or unusual letter patterns: EERIE, PARER, JAZZY, LEVEL, ABBEY, KAYAK, CYNIC, VIVID, SISSY, MUMMY, and similar. EERIE is the canonical example.

What they have in common:

- **Repeated letters**, especially two different repeats or a repeat the player hasn't confirmed — the feedback mechanics make a second copy easy to miss. EERIE (three E's), LEVEL, ABBEY, SISSY, MUMMY, VIVID all qualify.
- **Rare or awkward letters** (J, Z, Y, V, K, W, X, Q) in uncommon positions, which early guesses rarely confirm — JAZZY, KAYAK, CYNIC.
- **Unusual vowel structure** — vowel-heavy (EERIE) or vowel-light, or vowels in odd slots.
- **Near-miss traps**: words sharing many letters with common words but differing in one position, so the candidate set narrows slowly.

These are empirical regularities from how the feedback works, not measured rankings.

No — not in the direction you'd expect, and the effect is weak.

Hard Mode is a self-selected constraint chosen by a stable minority of committed players, so the hard-mode *share* is driven mainly by player composition, not by the day's word. If anything, the relationship runs slightly the other way: on genuinely hard words, casual players are more likely to fail or abandon, and casual players are the ones least likely to be in Hard Mode, so the hard-mode fraction can tick up marginally on hard days simply because the reporting pool shifts toward committed players.

But this is a small compositional effect, easily swamped by day-to-day noise and by which players happen to report. There is no strong, reliable tendency for hard words to draw more Hard Mode play. This is an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

Yes, but modestly, and it is a secondary effect.

People share results when they have an emotional hook — pride at beating a brutal word, or frustration/amusement at a controversial one (a word seen as obscure, offensive, or unfair). So genuinely hard words (EERIE-type) and controversial words do lift posting somewhat, because the shared result carries a story.

But this effect is smaller than the calendar and news-cycle drivers. The biggest surges come from external events (media coverage, holidays, collective downtime), not from the word itself. Word-driven bumps are real but typically marginal against day-of-week and news effects, and they are hard to separate from noise in the daily counts.

Retrying the same day is essentially impossible in the official game — Wordle gives one puzzle per day, and a failed attempt ends that day's game with no replay. So "retry the same day" is not a real behavior in the NYT version; only unofficial clones or archived/other-language versions allow it.

Playing the next day is very common. Wordle's daily-habit design is its core retention mechanism: the streak counter and the one-puzzle-per-day cadence push players to return the following day regardless of the previous outcome. A single failure typically does not break the habit — most players who fail still come back the next day, and many are motivated to "redeem" the loss or protect their streak.

So: same-day retry ≈ negligible (not offered); next-day return ≈ the large majority of players, including those who failed. This is an empirical judgment about game design and habit, not a measured figure.
